abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) have drawn substantial scientific attention due to their profound biological and economic impacts, especially in the context of climate change. This study highlights the crucial role of tropical cyclones (TCs) in disrupting MHWs by altering ocean temperatures. As demonstrated by Tropical Cyclone Bavi, intense sea surface temperature (SST) cooling, reaching up to 7°C, immediately terminated a mature MHW and suppressed subsequent MHW development for up to 8 months. More generally, on the basis of post-TC MHW cases (reoccurring within 1 month) during 2014 to 2023, we found that MHW disruption duration is proportional to the magnitude of TC-induced SST cooling, ~5 to 7 days per degree of cooling. At a broader scale, a 20-year (2004 to 2023) analysis revealed 99% significant inverse relationships between seasonal MHW and TC activity. These findings suggest that TCs can act as natural regulators, effectively mitigating heat stress from MHWs and potentially serving as a lifeline for marine ecosystems.
Tropical cyclones alone can destroy marine heatwaves and delay their formation by 5 to 7 days per degree of sea surface cooling.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: As the global average temperature record has been constantly reset in recent years due to the increasing concentration of greenhouse gases (1), extreme temperature events occur more often than at any time in history (2–6). These extreme events can exert adverse impacts on the environment, as well as the human society. Given the increasing number of high-impact events worldwide (7–13), marine heatwaves (MHWs; see the definition in Materials and Methods) have drawn high attention from researchers in recent years (3, 14). Accompanying a period of consecutive anomalously warm ocean temperatures, MHWs have prominent, sometimes devastating, consequences on marine ecosystems in many aspects. For example, the long-lasting warm water temperatures can lead to the bleaching of corals and the large-scale vanishing of seagrass fields (15–18); both serve as essential habitats and feeding grounds for marine organisms (19). The structure and community of species in the area struck by MHW or nearby areas are expected to shift and be modified markedly as different species have different tolerances to heat (20–22). Moreover, these ecological impacts would immediately result in socioeconomic consequences. For example, fisheries, aquaculture, and even the tourism could be substantially affected by the changing ecosystem due to MHWs (19, 23, 24). The effects of MHWs can be disastrous and far-reaching; understanding the mechanisms for their formation, development and dissipation is, therefore, a pressing issue.

Over the past decade, the causes of MHWs have been extensively studied (25). It is clear that MHWs are driven by atmospheric and/or oceanic processes through local or remote forcing. Increased solar insolation, reduced surface wind speed, and warmed air temperature associated with quasistationary anticyclonic pressure systems are the common drivers from the atmosphere (26–28). From the ocean, air-sea heat flux, current advection, and stratification are considered as the main players (11, 27, 29–31). Note that these atmospheric and oceanic drivers more often work simultaneously to heat up the ocean and generate MHWs. Recently, Pun et al. (32) suggested that tropical cyclones (TCs) can contribute to the development of MHW events. The subsidence region at the TC periphery tends to favor the presence of clear skies with lower surface wind speed. This situation substantially enhances the incoming solar radiation and reduces surface heat fluxes, favoring the formation of MHWs. Pun et al. (32) also found that such type of MHW, in turn, aided the subsequent TC’s intensification through the air-sea heat flux feedback mechanism. To our understanding, works on the interaction between these two kinds of extreme natural phenomena, i.e., MHWs and TCs, are still in its premature stage (32–36).

To date, most studies have primarily focused on identifying the mechanisms behind the formation and development of MHWs, with relatively less attention devoted to investigate the causes of their dissipation. Understanding the factors contributing to MHW dissipation is equally important as these factors can influence the duration of MHWs, which is directly tied to the severity and harmfulness of such events. On the other hand, these dissipation factors can be timely relief from the heat stress for marine life. Recent studies have noticed that MHWs are very likely to dissipate following the passage of TCs (32, 34). This is due to the pronounced sea surface cooling associated with the strong vertical mixing induced by TCs (37–49). However, detailed investigations of what the extent TCs can dissipate or disrupt MHWs are still lacking in the existing literature.

In this study, we will first present a case study of Tropical Cyclone Bavi, which completely eliminated an MHW in the East China Sea (ECS) in 2020 by generating substantial sea surface temperature (SST) cooling. Following this event, no more MHWs occurred again in this area for the rest of the year. Second, on the basis of a systematic statistical analysis with 85 well-defined TC-MHW cases identified in the western North Pacific during 2014 to 2023, we demonstrate that the duration of MHW interruption, if they reemerge in the post-TC period, depends on the magnitude of TC-induced SST cooling. Furthermore, analysis of the 20-year dataset (2004 to 2023) reveals that seasonal MHW activity is strongly modulated by TC activity. These findings provide clear evidence that TCs can act as effective regulators of MHWs, potentially mitigating their impacts on marine ecosystems.

sec.title: Disruption of MHW by Bavi
sec.p: In 2020, Bavi intensified to its peak intensity (100 knots or 51.4 m s−1) in the ECS and became the strongest TC in the region in the past decade. The rare intensification was found to be linked to an MHW preexisting on Bavi’s path (32). From the daily SST evolution in the ECS in late August 2020 (fig. S1), it is found that this MHW (indicated by “x” symbols) gradually developed around mid-August. A few days later (i.e., 19 to 24 August; fig. S1, E to J), it became more pronounced and covered a larger area. However, the MHW dissipated quickly after the passage of Bavi (i.e., 25 to 26 August; fig. S1, K and L).

For a quantitative comparison, we define 21 August and 26 August as the reference times before and after the TC, respectively. The SST map from 21 August reveals that the entire ECS was extremely warm before the TC, with SST values well above 30°C (Fig. 1A). Compared to the climatology, it is found that the SST anomalies, which are usually used to refer to the magnitude of MHWs when they happen (50), reached up to 3°C, expanding from the southwest of the Korean Peninsula (Fig. 1B). A large area of SST well exceeded the 90th percentile of the long-term daily values, indicating the presence of an MHW (Fig. 1C). Note that not all of this area (>90th percentile) is qualified as an MHW because it must also meet the minimum persistence requirement of 5 days. Nevertheless, the pre-TC ocean condition in the ECS was dominated by a prominent MHW, providing a favorable environment for TC intensification. By contrast, the SST map from 26 August illustrates that, right after the passage of Bavi, the MHW completely disappeared and replaced with a patch of cold SST (~22°C), particularly on the right-hand side of the TC track along the west coast of the Korean Peninsula (Fig. 1D). The SST dropped to 5°C below the climatology, or 3°C lower than the 10th percentile level of the long-term-averaged daily values, suggesting the occurrence of a potential cold spell (Fig. 1, E and F). This result clearly illustrates Bavi’s effective role in destroying a mature MHW along its path.

sec.p: It is well known that TC-induced vertical mixing with colder, deeper water primarily drives the decrease in SST. The SST cooling on 26 August 2020 with respect to the SST on 21 August 2020 is shown in Fig. 2A. It can be seen that Bavi generated marked SST cooling in the ECS. The maximum magnitude of the SST cooling was up to 7°C, located southwest of Jeju Island. In addition to the high wind speeds, the strong SST cooling was also likely attributed to the presence of semipermanent cold subsurface water in the ECS (51, 52). This intense SST cooling erased the warm anomaly and brought the SST below the 10th percentile (Fig. 1F).

sec.p: The impact of TC-induced SST cooling on subsequent MHW development and behavior is of particular importance and the focus of the present study. Notably, following the Bavi-induced cooling event, almost no MHWs reemerged in the affected area, as delineated by the 3°C SST cooling contour in Fig. 2B, for the rest of the year. However, a huge contrast is outside the cooling area, where up to 20 days of MHWs occurred in the northwest and southeast regions adjacent to the cooling zone. In the southern latitudes near Taiwan and the east of the Korean Peninsula, the cumulative MHW days can reach 30 for the rest of 2020. This indicates that large-scale environmental conditions were still favorable for MHW development. In addition, the area experiencing intense SST cooling took a substantially longer time, on average about 240 days (~8 months), to produce another MHW (Fig. 2C). In other words, MHW activity in this region was suppressed until April of the following year.

To further explore the impact of TC-induced SST cooling on MHW dissipation and subsequent development, the evolution of SST averaged over the main MHW area along the Bavi’s track was analyzed (fig. S2, A and B). It is observed that the MHW gradually developed before the TC but collapsed almost instantly when the TC arrived (fig. S2A). Again, this is due to the strong SST cooling (~7°C) induced by the TC. As a result, SSTs dipped below the 10th percentile, although this situation only lasted for 2 days. From the extended time series, it is found that, despite some fluctuations shortly after the TC, the post-TC temperatures remained low and lingered around the 10th percentile curve until early October (fig. S2B). However, the SSTs were still below the climatological values until mid-November. Even if the SSTs appeared to return to normal at the end of 2020, no qualified MHWs were established. For comparison, the SST time series during a similar period (i.e., from mid-July to the end of August) in 2016 was analyzed (fig. S2C). The year of 2016 was chosen because the ECS experienced one of its warmest Augusts (30) and the TC activity in the ECS was quiet during that period. Therefore, it provides an opportunity to differentiate the influence of TCs on MHW dissipation. During this period, two MHW events were identified, i.e., 23 July to 1 August 2016 (lasting for 10 days) and 10 to 26 August 2016 (lasting for 17 days). These two MHWs were close together, with only 5 days whose SSTs were just slightly below the 90th percentile threshold in between (fig. S2C). Compared to the short-lived MHW (6 days) encountered by Bavi in 2020 (fig. S2A), it is suggested that MHWs can last substantially longer in the ECS without the interference of TCs. According to this comparison, the duration of the MHW was reduced by about 65%, i.e., (1−617)×100% , due to the influence of TCs, highlighting the crucial role of TCs in modulating MHW activity.

As noted above, MHW development within the cold wake region following Bavi’s passage appeared to be suppressed for up to 8 months. Because atmospheric conditions also plays a crucial role in MHW formation, this prolonged MHW suppression may have been partially influenced by unfavorable atmospheric factors. To clarify the atmospheric contribution, we examined atmospheric conditions using the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) fifth generation of atmospheric reanalysis (ERA5) dataset (see Materials and Methods). In particular, surface net shortwave radiation (SWR) and 10-m wind speed (U10) were analyzed as these parameters are commonly recognized as key atmospheric drivers of MHWs (53, 54). During the 8-month period from 27 August 2020 (immediately following Bavi’s passage) to 30 April 2021 (when an MHW event reappeared in the cold wake area), four distinct MHW episodes were identified in the ECS. These occurred in November 2020, February 2021, March 2021, and April 2021, respectively (Fig. 3). Notably, during the first three episodes, MHWs were only observed in regions surrounding the cold wake, whereas SSTs within the cold wake still remained relatively low (Fig. 3, A to C). According to the reanalysis data, the cold wake region exhibited large-scale positive anomalies in SWR during the first three MHW episodes, suggesting generally favorable conditions for MHW development (fig. S3, A to C). However, the surface winds were less supportive, with negative values appearing only during the March 2021 event (fig. S4, A to C). Note that negative wind anomalies are considered favorable conditions as they limit heat loss to the atmosphere through reduced enthalpy fluxes. These findings indicate that atmospheric conditions during the first three MHW episodes were generally conductive to MHW development. Therefore, the prolonged absence of MHWs within the cold wake region is unlikely attributed to unfavorable atmospheric forcing.

sec.p: Another notable evidence appears in the final MHW episode in April 2021, when the cold wake region eventually experienced an MHW event (Fig. 3, D to F). During this period, atmospheric conditions were generally favorable, with positive SWR anomalies (fig. S3, D to F) and negative wind speed anomalies prevailing across the ECS (fig. S4, D to F). However, the onset of MHWs within the cold wake region markedly lagged behind that of the surrounding waters. This delay further highlights the suppressive effect of Bavi-induced SST cooling on subsequent MHW formation, even under otherwise favorable atmospheric conditions.

Moreover, to better characterize favorable atmospheric conditions, we proposed a simple index, referred to as the atmospheric condition index (ACI), based on the parameters of SWR and U10 (see Materials and Methods). As shown in fig. S5, the areal-averaged ACI over the ECS reveals that consecutive favorable atmospheric conditions, as reflected by positive ACI values, were intermittently present throughout the post-Bavi period. This finding further supports the notion that atmospheric forcing was unlikely the limiting factor inhibiting MHW formation in Bavi’s cold wake. Therefore, the prolonged MHW suppression is more likely attributable to the SST cooling induced by Bavi.

sec.title: Statistical analysis of 85 cases during 2014 to 2023
sec.p: To obtain more general conclusions, a larger group of samples was extracted from the peak TC seasons (July to October, referred to as JASO) in the western North Pacific between 2014 and 2023 for statistical analysis. This dataset consists of 85 well-defined TC-MHW interaction cases originating from 65 TCs during the 10-year period (Fig. 4, A and B). It is worth noting that rigorous selection procedures were performed to ensure that all of these 85 cases are associated with an obvious MHW under the TC track area (see Materials and Methods). According to their locations, these cases are further separated into three basin groups, namely, the ECS, the South China Sea (SCS), and the western Pacific (WP), for interbasin comparisons. All the cases with the key TC-MHW parameters with respect to different basins are summarized in tables S1 to S3. Because of the smaller area and naturally less TC activity, the ECS has only eight TC-MHW cases identified during 2014 to 2023, whereas the SCS and the WP contain 23 and 54 cases, respectively.

sec.p: The duration of pre-TC MHWs varied substantially ranging from 5 days, the MHW threshold, to 62 days, the one associated with Tropical Cyclone Chan-Hom in the WP in 2020 (Fig. 4A and table S3). On average, the duration of pre-TC MHWs appears to be longer in the WP (14.7 days) followed by the SCS (10.6 days), and then the ECS (9 days) (Fig. 5A). It is important to note that all of these MHWs rapidly dissipated after hit by a TC due to the TC-induced SST cooling (Fig. 4C), except one case associated with Tropical Cyclone Noul in the SCS in 2020. We found that the SST cooling induced by Noul was relatively small (~0.8°C), making it insufficient to offset the abnormal SST warming (fig. S6). From the mean values of SST cooling in different basins (Fig. 5B), it is found that the ECS exhibits the strongest SST cooling (3.1°C), which is substantially greater than the SCS (1.6°C) and WP (2.0°C). In addition to the presence of intrinsically cold subsurface water, as illustrated by the Bavi case (32), the strong SST cooling in the ECS is also attributed to the relatively higher mean TC intensity in the dataset (Fig. 5C). On the other hand, the relatively weak mean TC intensity partly explains the smaller SST cooling observed in the SCS. Evidently, because of the cooler ocean conditions left by TCs, the total number of subsequent MHW days for the rest of the year appears lowest in the ECS (~6 days), in stark contrast to the SCS (~16 days) (Fig. 5D). The WP appears in between, with an average number of subsequent MHW days of about 11 days, but exhibiting greater variation.

sec.p: Because long-lived MHWs exert much greater stress on marine ecosystems, it is important to assess how long a break of an MHW event can be interrupted by a TC. Such an MHW-free period could provide timely relief for marine life. Note that nearly half (40 cases) of the 85 TC-MHW cases never experienced MHWs again after the TC passage for the rest of the year (tables S1 to S3). In other words, these 40 MHWs were completely terminated by TCs. For the remaining 45 cases, MHWs reoccurred, and the mean MHW break following TC’s passage appears to be shortest in the ECS (22 days), despite the region favoring stronger SST cooling (Fig. 5E). In contrast, longer MHW breaks exhibit in the SCS (41.2 days), followed by the WP (35.4 days). Notably, the recurrence rate in the SCS reaches 82.6%, indicating a high likelihood of MHWs reoccurring after being disrupted by TCs in this region (Fig. 5F). This percentage is substantially higher compared to the ECS and WP, where post-TC MHW occurrence probabilities are 37.5 and 42.6%, respectively. The high recurrence rate in the SCS corresponds to the greater number of post-TC MHW days (Fig. 5D).

However, it should be noted that these MHW-free periods, especially those with a prolonged duration, may not be solely due to the impacts of TCs. Although the Bavi case demonstrates the potential for extended suppression (Fig. 3), other large-scale factors, such as atmospheric conditions, may also contribute. To further minimize the influence of such factors on MHW suppression, we focused on cases where MHWs reoccurred within 30 days (i.e., within 1 month) following a TC’s passage. This selection criterion assumes that the large-scale environment remained generally favorable for MHW development, making TC-induced SST cooling the dominant factor. Using this constraint, we identified 24 cases, and their corresponding atmospheric conditions were relatively favorable before and after the TCs, as indicated by positive ACI values (see Materials and Methods; figs. S7 and S8). The return period of MHWs is found to be strongly correlated with the magnitude of SST cooling (R = 0.75, P < 0.0003; Fig. 4D). On average, 1°C of SST cooling leads to approximately a 5-day delay in MHW reformation. If we further constrain the analysis to cases with a long duration of pre-TC MHWs (i.e., ≥10 days), which implies favorable preexisting environmental conditions, the correlation strengthens to R = 0.77 with P < 0.0006, and the disruption rate increases to about 7 days per degree of SST cooling (Fig. 4E). These strong correlations clearly highlight the critical role of TC-induced SST cooling in modulating post-TC MHW development.

sec.title: Correlations between seasonal MHW and PDI
sec.p: The above results clearly demonstrate that TCs can serve as an efficient natural terminator of MHWs. Therefore, TC activity would very likely influence MHW activity at seasonal or longer timescales. To identify this connection, annual maps for the total number of MHW days with the cumulative TC power dissipation index (PDI; see Materials and Methods) (55) in the western North Pacific during JASO over the 20-year period from 2004 to 2023 were generated (Fig. 6). It is found that the seasonal MHW patterns vary substantially from year to year. This variability is likely influenced by large-scale atmospheric systems or climatic events, such as El Niño or La Niña (56–58). However, the sign of TC’s modulation is noticeable. For instance, the ECS and ambient areas exhibited strong seasonal cumulative PDI in 2015, 2019, and 2020, substantially inhibiting MHW development. On the contrary, the strong PDI signals in 2006, 2010, and 2023 were confined to the south of the ECS and the north rim of the SCS, allowing MHWs to thrive in the ECS and SCS.

sec.p: On the basis of the 20-year (i.e., 2004 to 2023) PDI composite during the JASO period, six subregions (i.e., ECS, SCS, WP1, WP2, WP3, and WP4) are defined for correlation analysis (Fig. 7). It is worth noting that the highest PDI occurs east and northeast of Taiwan, indicating a substantial transfer of TC energy into these waters. The correlations between the regional mean MHW day count and PDI are shown in Fig. 8. All regions, except the SCS, exhibit a strong negative correlation between seasonal MHW and PDI. The correlation coefficients in the regions of ECS, WP1, WP2, and WP3 are particularly high and statistically significant (R ≤ −0.57, P < 0.01). This result indicates that TCs play a crucial role in modulating seasonal MHW activity in these regions. The lack of correlation in the SCS region, however, may be attributed to its complex hydrological conditions and nonlinear interactions between TCs and internal waves, as suggested by Guan et al. (59). On the other hand, the SCS lies at the center of the Asian summer monsoon region. Consequently, the weather and ocean temperatures over the SCS are strongly influenced by large-scale climate modes (60, 61). In particular, the low-level northwest Pacific anomalous anticyclone (NWP-AAC), driven by nonlocal SST forcing from the equatorial Pacific and Indian Ocean during and after El Niño years, is regarded as a fundamental mode (62, 63). The NWP-AAC not only modulates rainfall and SST but also affects TC activity in the region during summer (64, 65). A recent study further suggested that, owing to suppressed convection, the NWP-AAC can facilitate MHW development by enhancing solar insolation and reducing surface heat flux from the ocean to the atmosphere (66). The dominance of such a large-scale mode, through nonlocal air-sea interactions, may obscure the local relationship between TC and MHW activity in the SCS. Nevertheless, the influence of TCs on MHW activity in the SCS can still be observed in certain years, such as 2010, 2015, and 2023 (Fig. 6), supporting the idea that TC-induced SST cooling suppresses MHW development. The relationship between TC and MHW activity in the SCS warrants further investigation in the future.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Using Tropical Cyclone Bavi (2020) as a case study, we have demonstrated that a mature MHW was immediately terminated by strong SST cooling, which reached up to 7°C. This premature termination resulted in a 65% reduction in the MHW duration compared to a similar period without TC interference. We found that the cold wake of Bavi substantially inhibited subsequent MHW development for as long as 8 months. This is evident from observations showing that, although three to four MHW events occurred in the surrounding areas during this period, none developed within the cold wake region (Fig. 3).

To draw more general conclusions about the role of TCs in MHW dissipation, we conducted a systemic analysis using 85 well-defined TC-MHW cases identified during the peak TC seasons (i.e., JASO) from 2014 to 2023 in the western North Pacific (see the case selection procedure in Materials and Methods). The results reveal that 99% of MHWs (84 of 85 cases) disappeared following TC passage, showing compelling evidence that TC-induced SST cooling is a major mechanism for terminating MHWs. Furthermore, in 47% of the cases (40 of 85), no MHW reoccurred in the affected region for the remainder of the year, indicating that these events were essentially ended by TCs. In the remaining 53%, i.e., MHWs reappeared after the TC, the recovery time, or the duration of MHW disruption, was influenced by both ocean cooling and large-scale atmospheric conditions. To better isolate the effect of TC-induced SST cooling, we focused on a subset of fast recovery cases in which MHWs reoccurred within 1 month after TC passage. This subset accounted for 28% of all cases (24 of 85) and was characterized by favorable atmospheric conditions, as indicated by our newly proposed ACI (see Materials and Methods). In these cases, we found that the duration of MHW disruption was significantly correlated with the magnitude of SST cooling (R ≈ 0.75, P < 0.0006; Fig. 4, D and E). On average, under favorable atmospheric conditions, 1°C of SST cooling tends to extend MHW disruption by ~5 to 7 days.

In addition, we conducted a long-term investigation using 20 years of data from 2004 to 2023 to examine the relationship between MHW and TC activity at a broader scale. On the basis of our modified PDI, which incorporates TC structural characteristics to more accurately represent the spatial distribution of TC destructiveness (see details in Materials and Methods), we found statistically significant inverse correlations (R ≈ −0.6, P < 0.009) across much of the western North Pacific, except the SCS, where the MHW reoccurrence probability exceeds 80%. These strong correlations explicitly underscore the crucial role of TCs in modulating MHW activity. These statistical results are highly consistent with those derived from an independent dataset, i.e., the Optimally Interpolated SST (OISST) from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) (see Materials and Methods), regardless of whether a 30-year (fig. S9) or a 40-year (fig. S10) climatological baseline was used. This consistency suggests that our findings are robust and not sensitive to the choice of dataset or baseline period.

All in all, TC-induced SST cooling alone can destroy MHWs, but the reappearance of MHWs requires both favorable atmospheric and oceanic conditions. The duration of MHW disruption caused by TCs depends on the magnitude of SST cooling: Stronger SST cooling results in longer MHW interruption as the ocean needs more time to recover to pre-TC thermal conditions. During this recovery period, SST remains below the MHW threshold, thereby preventing MHW reformation. From a marine ecosystem perspective, these findings may be considered good news as TCs can not only pump up vital nutrients from deeper layers (67) but also act as timely rescuers, alleviating heat stress on marine organisms. A caveat is that the prolonged 8-month suppression observed in the Bavi case may represent an extreme scenario. How such cold SSTs can persist for this long time period, and the roles of other ocean drivers, such as currents and stratification, were beyond the scope of this study and remain to be explored. Furthermore, the extent to which TCs might help marine ecosystems overcome MHWs is still unclear and warrants further investigation. Nevertheless, our findings provide meaningful insights into TC-MHW interactions, which are critical for understanding their broader implications on marine ecosystems and disaster management, especially under the growing threat of anthropogenic climate change.

sec.title: SST and best-track datasets
sec.p: Being able to see through clouds, microwave SST is likely the most suitable satellite SST data in studying TC-ocean interaction (68). In this study, the microwave-based gridded OISST version 5.1 product generated and distributed by Remote Sensing Systems is used to identify MHWs as well as to investigate the effect of TCs. With the spatiotemporal resolution of daily and 0.25° × 0.25°, this OISST product combines SST measurements from all available microwave sensors for each day. In addition to regular quality controls, diurnal variation correction is applied at each quarter-degree grid (69, 70). The process ensures that the daily SST maps represent the foundation SST fixed at 12:00 UT, providing consistent SST data suitable for the longer-term study. The OISST dataset began in 1998, available on the website of Remote Sensing Systems (https://remss.com). For comparison, we also used the daily OISST dataset from the NOAA (71). With same quarter-degree spatial resolution, NOAA’s OISST is generated by combining satellite infrared and in situ observations. This dataset spans the period from 1981 to the present and is available from the US National Centers for Environmental Information (www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/optimum-interpolation-sst).

The information of TCs comes from the best-track dataset distributed by the US Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC). The best-track data provide the best estimates of postseason TCs at a 6-hourly interval. The parameters include position, intensity (i.e., maximum 1-min average sustained surface wind speed), minimum sea level pressure, wind radii, etc., used to characterize the TC (72). The data are available on JTWC’s website (https://www.metoc.navy.mil/jtwc/jtwc.html).

sec.title: Atmospheric reanalysis data
sec.p: To examine atmospheric conditions associated with MHW reoccurrence following a TC’s passage, we used the ERA5 (73) from the ECMWF. ERA5 is produced daily by a state-of-the-art forecast model and advanced data assimilation system (73). This global dataset offers high spatial (0.25° × 0.25°) and temporal (hourly) resolution and covers the period since 1940. Data are publicly available via the Copernicus Climate Change Service (https://climate.copernicus.eu/). In this study, we extracted surface net SWR and 10-m wind components (i.e., zonal and meridional) from ERA5. Wind speed (U10) was derived by combining the two wind components. To calculate daily anomalies, we first averaged the hourly data at four synoptic times (i.e., 00:00, 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00 UT) to obtain daily means. Then, a 30-year (from 1994 to 2023) daily climatology was constructed with the daily data. Last, daily anomalies were obtained by subtracting the climatology from each corresponding daily mean.

sec.title: Definition of MHWs
sec.p: The definition of MHWs is mainly based on Hobday et al. (50). Typically, an MHW event is identified when the local SST exceeds the upper 90th percentile of the long-term daily variation and this anomaly must persist for at least 5 consecutive days (cf. fig. S2A). In this study, the long-term daily climatology was generated on the basis of 26 years of OISST data spanning from 1998 to 2023. To increase the sample size, an 11-day window is applied. For example, the daily SST climatology on 20 August is the mean value of SSTs between 15 and 25 August during the 26-year period. Furthermore, if two MHW events are separated by less than 3 days, they will be considered as one consecutive event. This procedure will slightly affect the day count of the MHW. The calculation for the MHW was performed for each 0.25° grid cell.

sec.title: TC-MHW case selection
sec.p: Because TCs typically traverse thousands of kilometers over 1 or 2 weeks across the ocean, identifying specific regions where MHWs truly interact with TCs is challenging. In some cases, although MHWs may appear to coincide with a TC track, they may not necessarily be associated with the TC. This is because the MHW continues to evolve dynamically as the TC progresses along its path. If the MHW has dissipated long before the TC arrives, such an event should not be classified as a TC-MHW case. In addition, the uneven spatial distribution of MHWs across daily 0.25° grid points adds to the complexity of case identification. To minimize the ambiguity and enhance confidence, we used the Bavi case as a prototype for identifying TC-MHW interaction cases during the study period (i.e., JASO from 2014 to 2023). First, we examine the daily SST sequence maps from 5 days before the TC’s genesis through its dissipation (cf. fig. S1). If an obvious MHW signal is associated with the TC, we then identify the area of the MHW and classify it as a TC-MHW case (cf. the box in fig. S1). Second, a time series of areal averaged SST for the TC-MHW case is generated (cf. fig. S2). Last, key parameters, including SST cooling, pre-TC MHW duration, post-TC MHW day count, and MHW break (as shown in tables S1 to S3), are extracted from the time series for further analysis. This procedure ensures that all identified TC-MHW cases are well defined and representative. However, it should be noted that a single TC can have multiple TC-MHW cases, depending on the characteristics of the MHW and basins. A total of 85 TC-MHW cases were identified during the study period and are displayed in Fig. 4 (A and B).

sec.title: Power dissipation index
sec.p: TCs transfer momentum down to the ocean and cause ocean mixing, which is an effective mechanism to destroy MHWs. To investigate the influence of TCs on MHWs at the seasonal scale, we adopted the concept of PDI as proposed by Emanuel (55)

where V is the TC wind speed, and the period between t0 and t1 indicates the lifetime of the TC. The PDI relates the cube of the wind speed to the destructiveness and thus energy transfer to the ocean. Instead of integrating the maximum wind speed over a TC cycle as in Emanuel (55), we modified the PDI to allow it to represent spatial distribution with the consideration of TC’s structure. In other words, every 0.25° grid point has a PDI value relative to the position of the TC. Assuming an axisymmetric structure, the radial wind profile of the TC at each 6-hour interval is constructed on the basis of the three radii (i.e., 34, 50, and 64 knots) information available from the best-track dataset (45, 74). The spatial PDI for a TC is obtained by integrating the wind speed at each grid point (fig. S11A). Similarly, seasonal PDI is then to accumulate the PDI values within the season (i.e., JASO; fig. S11B). Note that the TC intensity lower than 34 knots does not have radius information; thus, we excluded those track points from the PDI calculation (fig. S11A). Because they are relatively weak and usually occur in onset and dissipation times, eliminating them will not affect the overall PDI patterns.

sec.title: Atmospheric condition index
sec.p: To characterize favorable atmospheric conditions for MHW development, we proposed a simple index, referred to as the ACI, based on two dominant atmospheric drivers, i.e., SWR and surface wind (U10), as suggested in (53, 54)
where ZSWR and ZU10 represent standardized anomalies of SWR and U10, respectively. The standardization is computed via

where x is the original value, whereas μ and σ are the mean and SD of the corresponding time series, respectively. The minus sign for ZU10 reflects the fact that lower wind speed promotes sea surface warming by reducing heat loss to the atmosphere. In this study, atmospheric conditions are considered favorable for MHW development when the ACI is greater than zero.

As demonstrated by the 2016 ECS MHW events, positive ZSWR and negative ZU10 anomalies are typically associated with the MHW periods (fig. S12A), highlighting the importance of these two atmospheric drivers. Notably, the newly proposed ACI effectively captures the periods of favorable atmospheric conditions under which MHWs may be able to develop (fig. S12B).

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The microwave-based OISST data are available from the Remote Sensing Systems (https://data.remss.com/SST/daily/mw/v05.1/netcdf/). The TC best track data are provided by the JTWC and are available on its website (https://www.metoc.navy.mil/jtwc/jtwc.html?western-pacific). ERA5 atmospheric reanalysis data are available via the Copernicus Climate Change Service (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/reanalysis-era5-single-levels?tab=download). NOAA’s OISST data can be obtained from the US National Centers for Environmental Information (https://ncei.noaa.gov/data/sea-surface-temperature-optimum-interpolation/v2.1/access/avhrr/).
